samples.brief: Two friends at a railway station discover their tickets are for different destinations.

content.title: Dos boletos diferentes
content.story:
Ana y Pablo están en la estación. Un tren llega. Ana tiene su boleto en la mano. Pablo tiene su boleto en una bolsa.

—¿Tienes tu boleto? —pregunta Ana.

—Sí, tengo mi boleto —dice Pablo.

Pablo abre la bolsa. Pablo saca el boleto.

—Mi boleto es para Madrid —dice Ana—. ¿Tu boleto también es para Madrid?

Pablo mira su boleto.

—No. Mi boleto es para Toledo.

Ana mira el boleto de Pablo. En el boleto dice: «Destino: Toledo». En el boleto de Ana dice: «Destino: Madrid».

—¡Tenemos boletos para destinos diferentes! —dice Ana—. Yo tengo un boleto para Madrid y tú tienes un boleto para Toledo.

—Pero yo quiero ir a Madrid contigo —dice Pablo.

Ana mira el reloj. Después, Ana señala una ventanilla. Una mujer está detrás de la ventanilla.

—Vamos a preguntar —dice Ana.

Pablo toma su bolsa. Los dos amigos caminan hacia la ventanilla con sus boletos.

Hand; Ana holds her ticket in her hand.

To open; abre means Pablo opens the bag.
To take out; saca means Pablo takes the ticket out of his bag.

For; introduces the destination a ticket is for.
Also or too; asks whether the other ticket is for the same destination.
To look at; mira describes looking at a ticket or the clock.
No; a negative answer.
Of or belonging to; links a ticket to its owner.

Different; diferentes describes destinations that are not the same.

To want; quiero means I want.
To go to; followed here by the desired destination.
With you; Pablo wants to travel with Ana.

Let's go and ask; suggests asking at the ticket window.

Both or the two; refers to Ana and Pablo together.
Friend; amigos is plural and refers to the two friends.
To walk; caminan means the two friends walk.
Toward; indicates the direction they walk.
With; they bring their tickets with them.

content.title: Dos pasajes diferentes
content.story:
Ana y Luis están en la estación. Ellos van a viajar juntos. Ana mira su pasaje.

—¿A dónde vas? —pregunta Luis.

—Voy a Valparaíso. ¿Y tú? —dice Ana.

Luis mira su pasaje. Él va a Rancagua.

—Nuestros pasajes son diferentes —dice Luis.

Ana mira el letrero de la estación. El tren a Valparaíso sale pronto.

—Vamos a preguntar en la boletería —dice Ana.

Los dos amigos caminan hacia la boletería. Una persona está detrás de la ventanilla. Ana tiene los pasajes en la mano.

strengths: Concrete present-tense clauses, explicit subjects and clear repetition closely follow the A1 guide.
The destinations are explicitly confirmed on both tickets, making the discovery easy to follow.
Definitions accurately cover contextual meanings, possessives, conjugated forms and useful phrases, including common words.
Walking to the ticket window leaves a natural unresolved next step.

materialIssues: “Ana tiene los pasajes en la mano.” — Luis previously holds and examines his own ticket; the unexplained transfer to Ana creates a small continuity gap.

“ir” — The explanation that all listed forms say where someone is going does not cover “van a viajar juntos” or “Vamos a preguntar”, which introduce actions. The separate construction note helps, but explicitly supports only the latter.
“pasaje” — The forms list omits “pasajes”, used twice in the story; explaining the plural would improve beginner support.

“Voy a Valparaíso” and “Él va a Rancagua.” — These establish intended destinations rather than explicitly showing the destinations printed on the tickets, making the requested ticket discovery less clear.

“Valparaíso”, “Rancagua” and “boletería” — These create an unsolicited Chile-specific setting despite the guide's caution against assuming Chilean Spanish. The wording itself is valid regional Spanish.
